title: Flat and Topological Floquet Minibands from Patterned Light in Untwisted Bilayer Graphene
abstract: Two-dimensional superlattices in van der Waals materials host flat bands and nontrivial topology, most famously at the so-called magic angles of twisted bilayer graphene, where flat bands give rise to correlated and topological phases. Yet these superlattices are usually created by twisting the layers or applying strain, and once a sample is fabricated, their period is fixed and extremely difficult to tune. Here we propose an alternative route: imprint the superlattice optically, using patterned electromagnetic fields rather than a physical twist or strain. We show that patterned in-plane cir- cularly polarized light and a combined drive consisting of a patterned out-of-plane longitudinal field and a uniform circularly polarized field produce isolated bands in both AA- and AB-stacked bilayer graphene. In AB stacking, the central bands additionally become nearly flat, capturing key features of a driven moir/'e superlattice. In this approach, the superlattice period is set by the illumination and is straightforward to tune, and circularly polarized light breaks time-reversal symmetry. Computing the valley Chern numbers of the central bands, we find a rich topological structure with several phase transitions in both stackings. Our results establish light-induced superlattices as a flexible and tunable platform for engineering flat bands and topological phases in bilayer graphene.
summary: The authors propose using patterned light fields as a tunable alternative to physical strain or twisting to create superlattices in bilayer graphene. By controlling the electromagnetic drive, they can independently modulate the electronic couplings, leading to the emergence of flat bands and measurable topological invariants like the Chern number. This establishes a highly flexible platform for realizing and studying moiré-like quantum phases.
main_problem: To find a flexible and tunable method to engineer flat bands and topological phases in bilayer graphene, bypassing the limitations of physically fixed strain or twisting.
main_result: Patterned electromagnetic fields allow for the independent and tunable control of intralayer and interlayer couplings, inducing isolated, nearly flat bands and rich topological structures characterized by calculable Chern numbers.
method: The study employs Floquet engineering by driving the system with patterned light fields, analyzing the resulting quasienergy band structure and topological invariants.
model_or_system: The system is untwisted bilayer graphene (AA- and AB-stacked) subjected to time-periodic driving from patterned in-plane and out-of-plane electromagnetic fields.
key_observables: Electronic band structure (minibands), quasienergy band structures, and valley Chern numbers.
important_parameters: Driving frequency ($\Omega$), superlattice period ($L$), and the relative strengths of the patterned fields ($a_0$).
main_assumptions: The analysis uses the Floquet-Bloch formalism and assumes the driving frequency is high enough to prevent overlap of Floquet replicas.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the band structures (quasienergy plots) under various driving conditions (circularly polarized, longitudinal, combined) as a function of driving frequency and superlattice period, alongside phase diagrams showing Chern numbers.
paper_structure: The paper systematically introduces the problem, details the optical coupling mechanisms (intralayer vs. interlayer), and then presents results comparing the topological outcomes (Chern numbers) and band flattening achieved using different combinations of patterned light drives.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the engineering of topological matter using external, tunable fields, which is highly relevant to open quantum systems and quantum optics approaches to condensed matter physics.

FIG. 2. Cartoon for illuminating bilayer graphene with a spa- tially patterned longitudinal light field generated by a vertical waveguide with a hexagonal array of apertures at the exit of the waveguide.
FIG. 3. Cartoon of simultaneous illumination of bilayer graphene with uniform circularly polarized and patterned lon- gitudinal light generated by a rectangular waveguide as de- scribed in Case 2.

FIG. 4. Stacking configurations of bilayer graphene. The A and B sublattices are shown in blue and orange, respectively. The intralayer nearest-neighbor hopping is denoted by γ and vertical bonds represent the interlayer coupling. (a) In AA stacking, each atom lies directly above the same sublattice in the opposite layer, giving interlayer hopping γ between A1–A2 and B1–B2. (b) In AB (Bernal) stacking, the upper layer is shifted so that A2 lies above B1, forming the dimer pair coupled by γ1, while A1 and B2 remain non-dimer sites.

FIG. 5. Evolution of the quasienergy band structure under increasing patterned circularly polarized drive. Panels (a)–(c) show AA-stacked bilayer graphene for a0 = 0.00, 0.10, and 0.25, respectively; panels (d)–(f) show AB-stacked bilayer graphene for a0 = 0.00, 0.07, and 0.12. In all cases, L = 100 nm and ¯hΩ= 3 eV. The quasienergy is plotted in units of EL, defined separately for the two stackings as described in the text: for AA we show (ε −γ)/EL with EL = ¯hvF |Km|, and for AB we show ε/EL with EL = (¯hvF |Km|)2/γ1.
